# Records that outrun their witnesses

Software agents now write most of what the Axiom Foundation publishes:
pre-registered forecasts, an append-only observation ledger, and
statutes encoded as executable rules. People review samples and
deterministic gates decide what merges, but no person witnesses every
record at the rate agents produce them. Whoever relies on those
records later — an auditor, a researcher, a court, the producer's own
future systems — needs a way to check them that does not depend on
having watched them being made.

The producer's infrastructure cannot supply that check. The producer
controls the repository, the CI configuration, the signing keys in its
own settings; anything the producer can reconfigure, a compromised or
careless producer can reconfigure to make bad history look good.
Monitoring fails for the same reason at a different layer: it watches
the producer's systems with the producer's access.

The receipt package takes the other route: custody. The producer
writes verifiable records as it works — chained manifests, timestamp
tokens, signatures, attestations — and any verifier with a clone of
the repository can later check the whole history offline, against
trust anchors the verifier committed in its own code. This paper
states what that check establishes (@sec-guarantees), why the design
follows from the threat (@sec-design), how the machinery earned its
way into one package (@sec-extraction), where it runs today
(@sec-production), and where it sits among adjacent systems
(@sec-related).

# What a verifier can conclude {#sec-guarantees}

A passing check tells the verifier four things about a record set,
each conditional on the specification and trust material the verifier
itself supplied [@receipt-repo]:

**History is append-only.** Every prior manifest, signature, and
receipt byte the trusted base contained is still present and
unchanged; new material extends the chain rather than rewriting it.
The release-chain verifier walks a contiguous, content-addressed
manifest history from genesis to head and compares it against the
exact recorded state; with a trusted base reference, it additionally
proves that no published release file changed bytes or file mode since
that ancestor.

**Nothing was backdated.** Each release carries RFC 3161 timestamp
tokens [@rfc3161] from the consumer's configured authorities, and the
verifier checks the token cryptographically against pinned root
certificates, policy identifiers, and signer identities — so the
record demonstrably existed before a time two independent-by-
configuration witnesses signed. A witness may record an authority as
unavailable; the verifier treats that as a verified declaration of
unavailability, never as proof from that authority.

**The producer signed it.** Ed25519 signatures verify against public
keys whose fingerprints live in the verifier's committed
specification. Keyrings support N-of-M thresholds and explicit legacy
generations: retired keys can vouch only for immutable history, never
for new material, and malformed or mispinned key material fails the
check outright rather than being skipped in favor of a sibling key
that happens to verify.

**Protected changes rode the declared workflow.** For commits that
touch a protected tree, the verifier checks workflow provenance
attestations against an anchored workflow identity, so the history of
the record surface itself carries evidence of how each change was
made.

The 0.5.0 release, open for review as of this writing, composes these
custody checks with a closed-world corpus binding: a witnessed journal
must describe exactly the working tree — an unlisted file, a missing
file, a rewritten byte, or a symlink where a regular file was recorded
each refuses — and a spanning `receipt verify` command runs custody,
binding, and declaration-completeness passes in order, stopping at the
first failure [@receipt-pr14].

The verdict is fail-closed in the strict sense the spanning verifier
documents: it is a pass only if every stage completed and every
required declaration was found; anything else, including an exception
the verifier did not anticipate, is a failure. The command renders
what it did *not* establish just as plainly — that any declared gate
actually passed, or that encoded rules read the law correctly —
because a verdict that lets a reader infer more than was checked is
worse than no verdict.

# Why the shape follows from the threat {#sec-design}

Each design rule answers a specific way verification could quietly
come to depend on the producer.

**Trust anchors live in the verifier's committed code.** Key
fingerprints, timestamp-authority roots, policy identifiers, content
roots, and required declarations sit in a specification file the
consumer commits and reviews. The package ships no defaults: there is
no configuration surface a producer could preload, and no environment
variable a deployment could quietly override. Signing keys are always
supplied by the caller; the package neither stores key material nor
reads trust configuration from the environment.

**Rotation is loud.** Replacing a key is a reviewed change to the
consumer's repository that moves the retired key into an explicit
legacy generation. Legacy keys verify immutable history only; new
material under a retired key refuses. There are no time-based
transition windows in which either key silently works.

**Verification runs offline on commodity tools.** A clone, Python,
OpenSSL, and Git suffice; nothing phones home, so the check works
against a producer whose infrastructure is unavailable — or
untrustworthy — at verification time. The one networked exception is
explicit: workflow-attestation checks call the GitHub CLI, and the
package's differential evidence for that surface is scoped accordingly
(@sec-extraction).

**Every gap is a refusal.** Missing witnesses, malformed rows,
unknown keys, out-of-range times, unlistable directories, paths that
escape the corpus root: each raises a typed error with the refusal
text preserved from the production system that first learned the
lesson. The libraries own no stdout or stderr; callers decide how to
render acceptance and refusal, and the exit code carries the verdict.

# The machinery {#sec-machinery}

Six modules ship in 0.4.0; the API reference at
[axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/) documents
them fully.

| Module | A pass establishes |
|---|---|
| `canonical` | One byte stream per value: canonical JSON with UTF-16 code-unit key order and ECMAScript number formatting, byte-compatible with the producer's TypeScript implementation. |
| `release_chain` | A contiguous, content-addressed, producer-signed, witness-receipted manifest history whose recorded state matches the working tree; with a base reference, byte-and-mode immutability of all published release files since that ancestor. |
| `append_gate` | A candidate change to an append-only ledger extends the trusted base exactly: prefix retained, rows valid, releases untouched, and any ledger append paired with exactly the next release set. |
| `sign` | Raw Ed25519 signatures over exact bytes; N-of-M thresholds over a domain-separated payload under consumer-pinned keyrings with explicit legacy generations. |
| `tsa` | One RFC 3161 token matches one consumer-pinned anchor — root bytes, policy, imprint, signed time, signer identity — via OpenSSL; witness sidecars follow the trust-bundle transition rules. |
| `attest` | GitHub's attestation service accepted the canonical subject for a commit under an anchored workflow identity; helpers enumerate protected-tree history and its enforcement epoch. |

The 0.5.0 review adds `corpus` (closed-world binding between a
witnessed journal and the working tree, plus gate-declaration
parsing), `verify` (the spanning pass ordering), and `cli`
(`receipt verify`, with text and JSON rendering and meaningful exit
codes) [@receipt-pr14].

# How the machinery earned its way in {#sec-extraction}

Three production systems built this machinery independently before the
package existed: pre-registered forecast records
[@brier-repo], an observation ledger's release chain [@ledger-repo],
and a signed statute corpus [@axiom-corpus-431]. Extraction, rather
than reimplementation, preserved something a rewrite would have spent:
the accumulated refusal behavior of verifiers that had already caught
real mistakes in production. The evidence standard varied with what
each surface allowed, and the repository publishes the evidence class
alongside the code. Four classes cover everything in the package.

**Byte-identical port.** The canonical-JSON module is the ledger's
file, verbatim: a test pins its SHA-256 against the recorded upstream
hash, so equivalence is identity.

**Differential extraction against the unmodified source verifier.**
The release-chain and append-gate surfaces (from the ledger) and the
witness and attestation surfaces (from the forecast system) came
across behind differential harnesses. Each harness pins the upstream
source files by SHA-256, runs the *unmodified* upstream verifier as an
oracle on live production fixtures — the forecast fixture alone
carries 53 snapshots, 52 witnesses, and 91 real timestamp tokens — and
requires the package to reproduce the oracle's verdicts, accepted and
refused alike, down to message bytes after two disclosed
normalizations (surrounding whitespace and volatile OpenSSL error-queue
identifiers). At the current review head the four harnesses run 94
cases, all passing.^[Local run at commit `c711adc`, 2026-08-10:
36 release-chain, 21 append-gate, 17 witness, and 20 attestation
differential tests. The attestation harness compares command
construction and outcome handling against a local stub and claims no
live-network equivalence.] The extraction-time evidence is also
published: the raw port diffs (633 and 695 lines) and three rounds of
independent review that requested changes twice before approving —
including an experiment that sabotaged base-tree materialization and
watched four differential cases fail, demonstrating the harness binds
the behavior it claims to bind [@receipt-receipts].

**Semantic adaptation of a production incident.** The signing module's
legacy-generation semantics come from the statute corpus, which learned
them the expensive way: rotating a release key had made previously
published, immutable releases unverifiable [@axiom-corpus-431]. The
fix — retired keys keep verifying the history they signed, only the
current generation signs anything new, and malformed key material is
always fatal — entered the package as a design adaptation with its own
direct tests. No differential oracle exists for this surface, and the
repository says so rather than implying one.

**New composition.** The 0.5.0 corpus binding, spanning verifier, and
CLI are new code composed from the extracted parts. They add no
cryptography and no trust anchors of their own; their evidence is a
refusal battery over the closed-world binding rules rather than an
upstream oracle [@receipt-pr14].

Publishing the taxonomy is part of the method. A single undifferentiated
claim — everything extracted, everything equivalent — would be simpler
and stronger-sounding, and wrong for two of the four classes. The
receipts directory carries the diffs, the review verdicts, and the
pinned hashes so a reader can place every module in its class without
asking us.

# In production {#sec-production}

As of August 10, 2026, three codebases pin and call the package on
their default branches or active custody branches: the Axiom encoder
delegates its apply-manifest verification to the package's threshold
keyring check; the forecast system's verifier and signer import the
package's signature primitives under a custody extra; and the
observation ledger's facts branch replaces its local verifier and
append gate with thin shims over the package, with the differential
harnesses re-run on every package change. The package's own
repository states the ledger consumes it in production; the
dependency pins and call sites are checkable in each repository.

The corpus-verification release extends the same custody discipline
from the producer's own systems to a published rule corpus. The pilot,
open for review in the New Zealand rule repository, commits a
verification specification — custody key, two timestamp-authority
anchors, content roots, required declarations — and a witnessed
journal of 104 rows binding 80 content files, 7 attested paths, and 17
gate declarations, so an outside auditor can run one offline command
over a clone and get a fail-closed verdict [@rulespec-nz-104]. Gate
rows are declarations: the verifier proves they were made and bound,
and states plainly that it did not rerun them.

# Related systems {#sec-related}

Each neighboring system solves an adjacent problem; the differences
below are checkable against their specifications.

RFC 3161 timestamping [@rfc3161] defines the single-token transaction
receipt builds on; the package composes saved tokens from multiple
configured authorities with pinned roots, policies, and signer
identities, and verifies them offline years later. Certificate
Transparency [@rfc9162] puts TLS certificates in public append-only
logs with third-party monitors; receipt verifies a repository-local
history against consumer pins without a log service, accepting the
narrower scope in exchange for no trusted log operator. The Update
Framework [@tuf-spec; @Samuel2010Survivable] also roots trust
client-side and supports thresholds and offline root keys, but is an
updater protocol for fetching current metadata; receipt checks an
already obtained clone's history and rotates roots only through the
consumer's reviewed specification. Sigstore [@Newman2022Sigstore]
binds signatures to OIDC identities via short-lived certificates and a
transparency log, and its bundles verify offline; receipt uses no
identity federation and no log, pinning long-lived producer and
authority identities per consumer instead. in-toto
[@TorresArias2019InToto] verifies that supply-chain steps matched an
owner-signed layout; receipt verifies custody of the records
themselves and treats process gates strictly as declarations it never
reruns. SLSA [@slsa-spec] specifies leveled requirements for build and
source integrity rather than a verifier; receipt is a concrete
verifier a consumer points at one history. Reproducible builds
[@reproducible-builds] compare independently rebuilt artifacts
byte-for-byte; receipt's differential harnesses compare verifier
verdicts on common fixtures, a related but distinct discipline. Signed
Git commits [@gitformat-signature] authenticate commit objects under
locally configured trust; receipt additionally verifies the
domain-specific chain, witnessed time, historical file bytes and
modes, and corpus binding.

The combination receipt occupies — per-consumer custody policy in
committed code, multi-witness timestamp composition, record-level
closed-world binding, and one fail-closed verdict that names its
non-conclusions — is, to our knowledge, not assembled elsewhere in one
offline-verifiable package.

# Scope and pending work {#sec-scope}

A pass establishes custody, not truth: declared gates were declared,
not rerun, and nothing in the verdict says encoded rules read the law
correctly. A stale clone that was honestly witnessed passes unless the
verifier supplies a trusted base reference or checks freshness out of
band. Timestamp-authority independence is configured, not proven: the
verifier enforces the anchor set the consumer pinned and cannot
establish that two authorities fail independently. The differential
harnesses cover finite fixture and mutation batteries, disclosed in
the tests, not all possible inputs. The waiver ratchet and chronology
tiers remain in their source systems pending extraction, and the
spanning CLI ships with the 0.5.0 release under review. The package is
Python; producers on other stacks interoperate at the artifact layer
(canonical JSON, manifests, tokens, signatures) rather than the
library layer.

# Availability

`receipt` is on PyPI (Apache-2.0), with source, port diffs, review
records, and differential harnesses at
[github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt](https://github.com/TheAxiomFoundation/receipt),
the package page at [axiom.org/receipt](https://axiom.org/receipt),
and the API reference at
[axiom.org/receipt/api](https://axiom.org/receipt/api/).
